title: On objective mismatch in molecular retrieval from tandem mass spectrometry
claim: Optimizing for one objective sacrifices the other: common training losses trace a Pareto front between proxy similarity and downstream retrieval.
layout: 1 scatter panel, labeled points joined by dashed line, callout labels
description: A single scatter plot with a light grid. The x-axis is HR@1, the retrieval hit rate, running from about 0.09 to 0.19. The y-axis is Tanimoto fingerprint similarity, running from about 0.08 to 0.22. Five light-blue dots, one per training loss, are joined by a gray dashed line. Each dot has a black leader line to a text label: IoU Loss, Cosine Loss, Binary Cross Entropy, Focal Loss and Contrastive Loss. IoU Loss sits top-left, with the highest Tanimoto and lowest HR@1. The points move right with slowly falling Tanimoto, then drop steeply to Contrastive Loss at bottom-right, which has the highest HR@1 and the lowest Tanimoto. The eye goes first to the steep downward slope at the right and the labeled endpoints. No point is highlighted as 'ours', so the plot shows a trade-off, not a win.
caption: Empirically, different loss functions form a Pareto front trading off fingerprint similarity (y-axis) and retrieval performance (in terms of hit rate @ 1, x-axis) on MassSpecGym. See [ref] for experimental details.
abstract: Identifying molecular structures from LC-MS/MS spectra is a central problem in computational metabolomics, often approached by predicting molecular fingerprints and retrieving candidates via similarity search. Despite widespread use, the relationship between training objectives for fingerprint prediction and downstream retrieval performance remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the alignment between these objectives and show that they can be misaligned under uncertainty. Adopting a decision-theoretic perspective, we derive novel regret bounds that characterize when Bayes-optimal predictors for fingerprint similarity diverge from those for molecular retrieval. Our analysis reveals that optimizing standard similarity-based losses can degrade retrieval performance, and that the extent of this mismatch depends on the similarity structure of candidate sets. Empirically, we validate our theory on the MassSpecGym and Enveda-180 datasets, observing a Pareto frontier between fingerprint accuracy and retrieval metrics across commonly used loss functions. These findings highlight potential trade-offs in fingerprint-based molecular identification and provide principled guidance for the design of learning objectives in small molecule mass spectrometry.
